newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian share market looks westward, eyes Fed.
newsitem.headline: Russian share market looks westward, eyes Fed.

text.p: The Russian share market has shifted its gaze westward from its traditional domestic focus and dealers say it is set to track the world's major markets if U.S. interest rates rise on Tuesday.
With its dominance by foreign investors, the market has traditionally shuddered when President Boris Yeltsin sneezes while ignoring a raft of Russian and foreign economic indicators.

But share prices in Russia are beginning to correlate with those in the West. Traders say deals have ground to a halt after Russia followed other markets down on fears of a U.S. short-term interest rate hike.

The market fears the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates on Tuesday following Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments last week stressing the importance of controlling inflation. Russian markets will be closed by the time the news emerges.
"The Federal Reserve is the deciding factor for Western investors now," said UFG trader Maxim Perlin. "Isn't it strange how the Russian market is showing more and more correlation with Western ones?"
Russian markets do not usually react to major foreign economic indicators and have been considered a special beast.

But share prices drifted on Monday as investors looked towards Washington. "All eyes are looking that way (at the Fed) at the moment. The only buyers are domestic Russian investors," said Peter Kizenko, chief equities trader at ING Barings.
Traders and analysts calculate that Western investors make up two-thirds to three-quarters of Russian share trading.

Short-term investors -- anywhere from 25 to 75 percent of the Westerners -- are decreasing their presence as hedge funds look elsewhere for high returns and are being replaced by more conservative institutions, they say.
Waves of such new investors changed the dynamics of the tiny Russian share market, which sees some $40 million turnover on a good day, in a New Year's rally which lasted two months.

Deep-pocketed foreign investors, such as U.S. mutual funds, poured money into the market, lifting the Russian Trading System 23-share index of leading shares to 349.27 at the end of February from under 200 at the end of last year.
But economists say institutional investors have now tuned in to listen to Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
"You are dealing with more cautious money," said Christopher Smart, director of research at Pioneer Securities in Moscow.

"The first investor wave was seeking to maximise return and was not scared of any risk. They were not as sensitive to what was happening in the U.S. Bigger funds are more risk sensitive," he said, adding interest rate fears prompted flight to quality.
He said Russia had always been linked to world markets to an extent, but fears of an interest rate hike had not arisen during Russia's long bull run.
Al Breach, an economist at the Russian European Centre for Economic Policy in Moscow, said interest rate fears affected hedge funds, still an important market force.
"There is basically a lot of cheap money about," he said. Hedge funds borrow cheaply from the Japanese banks and buy dollar-denominated emerging market debt or shares."
An interest rate hike could seriously affect their profits.

"A rise of 25 basis points in the U.S. (short-term interest rates) should not make any difference in Russia, but if it in turn means the U.S. markets start to sell off, if rates are seen rising to seven percent, you will see money start to come out."
Kizenko said the short money appeared readiest to flee.
"Right now the shorter term players are getting out but I have not seen the longer ones moving," he said.
CentreInvest Securities chief institutional trader Dan Rapoport said the trend was towards more conservative, institutional money.
"The trend is toward long money, because we are seeing a lot of hedge funds move out," he said.
